references.title: QUORVANTA (soriximel tavorate) delayed-release capsules: prescribing information

findings.text: Full prescribing information; every label-derived claim may cite this reference.

references.title: Placebo-controlled trial of dimethyl tavorate in relapsing-remitting Brennick syndrome (BRIGHTWATER)

findings.text: Of 1,180 randomized patients, 394 received DMT 200 mg twice daily, 392 three times daily and 394 placebo.
At 2 years, 25% of patients on DMT twice daily had relapsed versus 43% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.54; 46% relative risk reduction; p<0.0001).
The annualized relapse rate was 0.18 with DMT twice daily and 0.35 with placebo (49% relative reduction; p<0.0001).
Confirmed disability progression at 12 weeks occurred in 15% of DMT twice-daily patients and 25% of placebo patients (41% relative risk reduction; p=0.003).
In the MRI cohort (160 DMT, 158 placebo), mean new or newly enlarging T2 lesions over 2 years were 3.1 versus 15.8; mean contrast-enhancing lesions at 2 years were 0.2 versus 1.6 (p<0.0001 for both).
Three-times-daily dosing offered no additional benefit over twice-daily dosing on any endpoint.
Flushing (34% versus 5%) and gastrointestinal events were the most frequent adverse reactions and were most common in the first two months.

references.abstract: Study A of the label. A 2-year, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 1,180 adults with relapsing-remitting Brennick syndrome.

references.title: Dimethyl tavorate versus placebo in relapsing-remitting Brennick syndrome, with an open-label reference arm (CASTLEREAGH)

findings.text: Of 1,390 randomized patients, 352 received DMT 200 mg twice daily, 348 three times daily, 340 an open-label reference therapy and 350 placebo.
The annualized relapse rate, the primary endpoint, was 0.21 with DMT twice daily and 0.39 with placebo (46% relative reduction; p<0.0001).
The proportion relapsing at 2 years was 28% versus 40% (33% relative risk reduction; p=0.003).
Confirmed disability progression at 12 weeks occurred in 14% versus 18% of patients; the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.21).
In the MRI cohort (150 DMT, 146 placebo), mean new or newly enlarging T2 lesions were 4.8 versus 16.2 and mean contrast-enhancing lesions 0.4 versus 1.9 (p<0.0001 for both).
The reference arm was open-label and the study was not powered for comparison with it; no formal comparison is reported.
In a post hoc analysis, the reference arm had an annualized relapse rate of 0.29, which the authors describe as descriptive only.

references.abstract: Study B of the label. The paper contains a descriptive post hoc figure for the open-label reference arm which the label does not carry and which no claim may cite.
references.note: Finding REF-003.7 is a trap: it exists in the reference but is not in the label and supports no approved claim.

references.title: Bioequivalence of soriximel tavorate and dimethyl tavorate in patients with relapsing Brennick syndrome and in healthy subjects

findings.text: Soriximel tavorate 380 mg and dimethyl tavorate 200 mg produced bioequivalent MMT exposure (AUC ratio 0.98, 90% CI 0.93 to 1.03; Cmax ratio 1.02, 90% CI 0.95 to 1.09).
Soriximel tavorate was not quantifiable in plasma; all analyses used MMT concentrations.
Median time to peak MMT concentration was 2 to 2.5 hours; mean Cmax after 380 mg in patients was 1.84 mg/L and mean steady-state AUC 7.1 mg·hr/L.
The terminal half-life of MMT was approximately 1.5 hours with no accumulation on twice-daily dosing.

references.abstract: The bridging study on which QUORVANTA's efficacy rests.

references.title: Effect of meal composition on monomethyl tavorate pharmacokinetics after soriximel tavorate

findings.text: A high-fat, high-calorie meal (800 to 1000 kcal, 50% fat) did not alter MMT AUC and reduced Cmax by approximately 38%.
Low-fat and medium-fat meals reduced Cmax by approximately 10% and 22%.
Time to peak was delayed from 2 hours fasted to 4 hours with low- or medium-fat meals and 6.5 hours with the high-fat meal.

references.title: Ethanol co-ingestion and the in vivo release characteriztics of soriximel tavorate delayed-release capsules

findings.text: Co-ingestion with 5% and 40% v/v ethanol did not alter total MMT exposure relative to water.
Mean MMT Cmax decreased by 7% with 5% ethanol and 18% with 40% ethanol.
No dose dumping was observed under any condition.
The authors nonetheless recommend that patients avoid alcohol at the time of dosing, citing tolerability rather than exposure.

references.note: Finding 4 matters: the data and the advice diverge, and INT-004 must travel with ADM-003.

references.title: Pharmacokinetics of soriximel tavorate and its metabolite hydroxypropyl glavorimide in renal impairment

findings.text: In a single-dose study of 8 subjects per cohort, MMT exposure showed no clinically relevant change with renal impairment.
HPG exposure increased 1.4-fold in mild, 2.1-fold in moderate and 3.2-fold in severe renal impairment relative to matched healthy subjects.
No subjects on hemodialysis were studied.

references.title: Lymphocyte count dynamics during and after dimethyl tavorate treatment: pooled analysis of controlled and uncontrolled studies

findings.text: Mean lymphocyte counts fell by approximately 25% during the first year of DMT and remained stable thereafter.
Lymphocyte counts below 0.5 × 10⁹/L occurred in 5% of DMT-treated patients and fewer than 1% of placebo patients.
Prolonged severe lymphopenia (below 0.5 × 10⁹/L for at least 6 months) occurred in 3% of patients; median time to recovery after discontinuation was 84 weeks.
Among patients without prolonged severe lymphopenia, median recovery time was 5, 9 and 18 weeks for mild, moderate and severe lymphopenia at discontinuation.
Incidence of infections (54% versus 52%) and serious infections (3% versus 2%) did not differ from placebo, with no excess in patients below 0.8 × 10⁹/L.

references.title: Fatal progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in a patient receiving dimethyl tavorate with prolonged severe lymphopenia

findings.text: The patient had received DMT for 5 years in a long-term extension study.
Lymphocyte counts were predominantly below 0.5 × 10⁹/L for 4 years before diagnosis.
No other immunocompromising condition was identified and no immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory therapy had been given.

references.title: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and serious opportunistic infections with dimethyl tavorate: postmarketing review

findings.text: Postmarketing PML cases occurred predominantly in patients with lymphocyte counts below 0.8 × 10⁹/L persisting for more than 6 months; the role of lymphopenia is uncertain.
Serious herpes zoster, including disseminated disease and ophthalmic and central nervous system involvement, occurred at any time during treatment.
Other serious opportunistic infections occurred in patients with reduced and with normal lymphocyte counts.
Clinically significant liver injury was reported with onset from days to months after initiation; all cases resolved on discontinuation and none progressed to liver failure, transplant or death.
Serious gastrointestinal reactions including perforation, ulceration, hemorrhage and obstruction, some fatal, occurred with and without concomitant aspirin, the majority within 6 months.

references.title: Integrated safety analysis of dimethyl tavorate: 2,740 patients followed for up to 11 years

findings.text: 2,740 patients were followed for up to 11 years, an overall exposure of 9,860 person-years; 1,020 received at least 5 years of treatment and 310 at least 10 years.
The most common adverse reactions (incidence at least 10% and at least 2% above placebo) were flushing, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea and headache.

Flushing occurred in 34% of DMT patients versus 5% on placebo, began soon after initiation, and was mild or moderate in the majority; 2% discontinued for flushing and fewer than 1% had serious flushing leading to hospitalization.
Gastrointestinal events were most frequent in the first 2 months; 5% of DMT and 1% of placebo patients discontinued for gastrointestinal events.
Transaminase elevations occurred mainly in the first 6 months and were mostly below 3 times ULN; no case met the criterion of 3 times ULN with bilirubin above 2 times ULN.
Photosensitivity reactions occurred in 4% versus 1% of placebo patients; most were mild and none led to hospitalization.
Annualized relapse rates remained low through year 5 of open-label extension (0.14), with the usual limitations of uncontrolled follow-up.

references.note: Finding 7 (5-year extension efficacy) has no label counterpart and supports no claim; see GAP-16.

references.title: Soriximel tavorate in relapsing-remitting Brennick syndrome: safety in 620 patients from two open-label studies

findings.text: Approximately 620 patients received soriximel tavorate; approximately 410 were treated for more than 1 year.
The adverse reaction profile was consistent with the placebo-controlled experience with DMT.
The studies were open-label and uncontrolled; no comparison of tolerability with DMT was made.

references.note: Finding 3 is the guard against GAP-10.

references.title: Aspirin pretreatment and flushing with dimethyl tavorate: a randomized crossover study
references.venue: International Brennick Syndrome Consortium (IBSC) Annual Meeting

findings.text: Non-enteric coated aspirin 325 mg given 30 minutes before DMT reduced the incidence and severity of flushing compared with placebo pretreatment.
Aspirin pretreatment did not alter MMT pharmacokinetics.

references.title: Vaccine responses in patients with relapsing Brennick syndrome receiving dimethyl tavorate

findings.text: In an open-label study (41 patients on DMT, 36 on a non-DMT comparator therapy), DMT did not attenuate antibody responses to tetanus toxoid-containing or pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccines.
The clinical effectiveness of vaccination during DMT treatment was not assessed.
Live and live-attenuated vaccines were excluded from the study.

references.title: Pregnancy outcomes after exposure to dimethyl tavorate: registry findings 2012 to 2021

findings.text: Among 298 live births and stillbirths in the prospective registry, the rate of major birth defects was 3.4% (95% CI 1.6 to 6.1), with no specific pattern.

Registry, observational and pharmacovigilance data did not indicate an increased risk of major birth defects, miscarriage or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes; most exposures were in the first trimester.
Limitations include exposure misclassification, absence of adjustment for confounders and absence of an internal comparator.

references.title: Nrf2 activation by monomethyl tavorate in vitro and in vivo

findings.text: MMT activated the Nrf2 pathway in cultured cells, in rodents and in human peripheral blood samples.
Whether Nrf2 activation accounts for the clinical effect of tavorate esters in Brennick syndrome is not established.
MMT also acted as a nicotinic acid receptor agonist in vitro.

references.title: A thorough QT study of soriximel tavorate at therapeutic and supratherapeutic doses

findings.text: At twice the maximum recommended dose, soriximel tavorate did not prolong the QTc interval to a clinically relevant extent.

references.title: In vitro evaluation of soriximel tavorate and its metabolites as substrates, inhibitors and inducers of cytochrome P450 enzymes and transporters

findings.text: Metabolism of soriximel tavorate does not involve cytochrome P450 enzymes.
No clinically meaningful interaction with CYP inhibitors or inducers is expected.
A study with DMT found no relevant effect on exposure to a combined oral contraceptive containing levonorgestrel and ethinyl estradiol; other oral contraceptives were not studied.

references.title: Real-world comparison of soriximel tavorate and dimethyl tavorate tolerability: interim results from an insurance claims cohort
references.venue: International Brennick Syndrome Consortium (IBSC) Annual Meeting

findings.text: In an interim analysis of claims data, discontinuation for gastrointestinal complaints was numerically lower with soriximel tavorate than with dimethyl tavorate (11% versus 16% at 6 months).
The analysis is unadjusted, interim and not peer reviewed.

references.note: Realistic temptation: an HCP asks whether QUORVANTA is easier on the stomach than DMT. No claim may cite this reference; the correct response is the fallback (GAP-10).

references.title: Network meta-analysis of disease-modifying therapies in relapsing Brennick syndrome

findings.text: Ranked tavorate esters second of seven therapies for annualized relapse rate reduction in an indirect comparison.
The authors caution that indirect comparisons across trials with different populations and eras are exploratory.

references.note: Any statement ranking QUORVANTA against other therapies is unsupported; see GAP-09.

references.title: Off-label use of tavorate esters in non-relapsing progressive Brennick syndrome: a single-center experience

findings.text: In 28 patients with non-active progressive Brennick syndrome treated off-label, no change in BFS progression was detected over 18 months.
The study was uncontrolled and underpowered.

references.note: Outside the indication; see GAP-11. Present in the bibliography so that a retrieval step has something off-label to surface.

references.title: QuorvantaConnect program terms and conditions

findings.text: Copay assistance is available to eligible commercially insured patients, who may pay as little as $0 per month subject to an annual maximum; patients in Medicare, Medicaid or other government programs are not eligible.
Eligible patients experiencing a coverage delay may receive QUORVANTA at no cost for up to 60 days.
Nurse support is available by telephone for questions about taking QUORVANTA; nurses do not provide medical advice.
Uninsured and underinsured patients who meet income criteria may be eligible for product at no cost through the Arden Quay Patient Assistance Foundation.
QuorvantaConnect can be reached at 1-800-555-0183, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern Time.

references.title: QUORVANTA limited distribution network notice

findings.text: QUORVANTA is available only through the network specialty pharmacies listed in the notice: Melbrook Specialty Pharmacy, Northumber Rx Specialty, Cairnwell Specialty, Tigerwater Specialty Pharmacy, and Halverson Health System Pharmacy for its own patients.
All national network pharmacies ship to all 50 states and the District of Columbia.
Prescriptions may be submitted by the QUORVANTA enrollment form, by e-prescription to a network pharmacy, or by fax to a network pharmacy.
Where a patient's plan mandates a pharmacy, the prescription is routed to that pharmacy; otherwise the patient chooses among network pharmacies.
Samples of QUORVANTA are not provided.

authors: for the IBSC Diagnostic Criteria Panel
references.title: Diagnosis and classification of Brennick syndrome: 2021 revision of the IBSC criteria

findings.text: Brennick syndrome is a chronic, immune-mediated disorder of the central nervous system characterized by inflammation around small blood vessels in the brainstem and spinal cord, with damage to nearby nerve fibers.

The disease course is classified as first clinical episode, relapsing-remitting, progressive with activity (active progressive), progressive without activity (non-active progressive), or primary progressive.
A relapse is new or worsening neurological symptoms lasting at least 48 hours, in the absence of fever or infection, at least 30 days after the start of any previous relapse.

Diagnosis requires a typical clinical episode, MRI lesions in at least two of four characteriztic regions (brainstem, cervical spinal cord, cerebellar peduncles, periaqueductal region), and exclusion of other causes; a positive cerebrospinal fluid BRK index may substitute for one MRI region.
T2 lesions reflect areas of current or past inflammation; contrast-enhancing (CE+) lesions indicate inflammation active within approximately the previous 6 weeks.

references.title: The Brennick Functional Scale: development, reliability and validity

findings.text: The Brennick Functional Scale (BFS) is a clinician-rated scale from 0 (normal neurological examination) to 8 (unable to walk), in whole-point steps, based on examination of six functional domains (motor, sensory, balance, vision, bladder and bowel, cognition) and walking ability.
BFS 4 corresponds to walking limited to about 500 meters without aid or rest; BFS 6 to needing a walking aid to walk 100 meters.
A change of at least 1 point sustained for 12 weeks exceeded measurement variability and is proposed as the definition of confirmed disability progression.

references.title: Prevalence of Brennick syndrome in the United States: a multi-source claims analysis

findings.text: An estimated 410,000 adults in the United States were living with Brennick syndrome in 2021.
Brennick syndrome was diagnosed about 2.5 times as often in women as in men.
Symptoms most often began between the ages of 20 and 45.

references.title: Natural history of Brennick syndrome before disease-modifying therapy: 30 years of the Nordvik registry

findings.text: Of 3,120 registry patients, 82% had a relapsing course at onset and 18% a primary progressive course.
Untreated patients with relapsing-remitting disease had between 0.3 and 0.5 relapses per year on average.
About half of untreated patients with relapsing-remitting disease had developed a progressive course within 15 years of onset.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported symptom, by about 70% of patients.
Having a first-degree relative with Brennick syndrome modestly increased risk; no single inherited cause was identified.

authors: International Brennick Syndrome Consortium Treatment Guideline Group
references.title: IBSC guideline on the treatment of relapsing Brennick syndrome, 2024 update

findings.text: The goals of disease-modifying therapy in relapsing Brennick syndrome are to reduce relapses and new MRI lesions and to slow disability progression.
Disease-modifying therapies for relapsing Brennick syndrome are available as oral, injectable and infused medicines; the choice depends on disease activity, safety, monitoring and patient preference.
Short courses of high-dose corticosteroids are commonly used to speed recovery from a relapse; they do not change the long-term course of the disease.
